title: La Villa De Paris - VS -SECP
text:
JUDGMENT SHEET 
ISLAMABAD HIGH COURT, ISLAMABAD 
JUDICIAL DEPARTMENT 
 
1. Writ Petition No.3566 of 2021 
 
 
La Ville De Paris Housing Scheme Limited 
Versus 
Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan and others 
 
 
2. Writ Petition No.4598 of 2022 
 
 
La Ville De Paris Housing Scheme Limited 
Versus 
Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan and others 
 
 
3. Writ Petition No.314 of 2023 
 
 
La Ville De Paris Housing Scheme Limited 
Versus 
Securities and Exchange Commission of Pakistan and another 
 
 
Petitioner by: 
M/s Shahbaz Yar Khan and Syed 
Asad Ali Shah, Advocates. (In all 
petitions) 
 
 
Respondents (SECP) by: 
Barrister Omer Azad Malik, Syeda 
Muneeza Fatima and Mr. M. Fasih 
Idrees, 
SPPs, SECP. (In all 
petitions) 
 
 
Date of Hearing:  
 
06.10.2025. 
 
 
INAAM AMEEN MINHAS, J.- This judgment shall decide the 
captioned three writ petitions arising out of the same controversy 
between the same parties. 
2. 
In writ petition No.3566/2021, the petitioner company, namely, La 
Ville De Paris Housing Scheme Limited, has assailed the Inspection 
Order dated 24.03.2021, issued under section 221 of the Companies Act,

2 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
2017 (“Act 2017”), Inspection Report dated 06.05.2021, Show Cause 
Notice dated 21.05.2021 issued under section 256 of Act 2017, Notice 
dated 09.06.2021 issued under section 474 of Act 2017 and Order dated 
21.09.2021 under section 474 of Act 2017, issued by the respondents i.e., 
Securities & Exchange Commission of Pakistan (“SECP”). 
3. 
Through writ petition No.4598/2022, the petitioner company seeks 
direction to the SECP to provide it attested copies of the NAB reference. 
4. 
In writ petition No.314/2023, the petitioner company has assailed 
the Order dated 12.01.2023, passed by the SECP, whereby its review 
application against Investigation Order dated 09.09.2022, under section 
256 of the Act 2017, was dismissed.  
5. 
The brief facts of the captioned writ petitions are that the 
petitioner company was incorporated as (Private) Limited Company with 
the SECP on 19.10.2020 and later converted into a Public Limited 
Company. Its principal line of business is to carry on business and 
management of Housing Estate Development as per clause 3(i) of its 
Memorandum of Association (“MOA”). The petitioner company applied 
for 
and 
was 
granted 
Preliminary 
Planning 
Permission 
(“PP 
Permission”) by the Gujranwala Development Authority (“GDA”) on 
25.08.2021 for a proposed housing scheme in District Gujranwala. 
Thereafter, the petitioner company started issuing registration certificates 
(Le Paris Registration Certificates) to its prospective members and 
customers, received advances for future residential and commercial 
properties and participation in lucky draw offering lucrative prizes.  The 
SECP, upon various intimations from print and electronic media 
regarding the petitioner company’s involvement in inviting the public to 
purchase the said certificates for future investments in the project of the 
petitioner company, took cognizance of the matter and ordered an onsite 
inspection of the petitioner company vide impugned Inspection Order 
dated 24.03.2021. To address the concerns of the SECP, the petitioner 
company publicly clarified that all amounts received, were advances

3 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
subject to GDA approval. The petitioner company submitted replies to 
all notices of SECP and sought a reasonable time due to COVID-19 
related constraints. Despite this, impugned Inspection Report dated 
06.05.2021 was issued without a physical inspection, followed by 
impugned Show Cause Notice dated 21.05.2021 for initiation of 
investigation into affairs of the company, and impugned Notice dated 
09.06.2021 and impugned Order dated 21.09.2021 u/s 474 of the Act 
2017. Later the petitioner company filed review petition against the 
investigation order dated 09.09.2022, which was dismissed vide 
impugned Order dated 12.01.2023. 
6. 
The learned counsel for the petitioner company contended that 
impugned Inspection Order, Inspection Report, Show Cause Notice, 
proceedings under section 474 of the Act 2017 and Order issued by the 
SECP are illegal, unlawful, and not sustainable in law or on facts, and 
therefore liable to be set aside. He submitted that the SECP acted 
arbitrarily, with bias and mala fide intent, without inspecting the 
petitioner company’s record despite repeated correspondence, and issued 
a false and baseless impugned Inspection Report, followed by impugned 
Show Cause Notice in violation of the principles of natural justice. He 
further submitted that no proper hearing or opportunity was provided, 
and that the SECP acted beyond its lawful authority, allegedly under 
business and political rivalries and unlawfully interfering with the 
petitioner company’s lawful business; that such actions infringe the 
fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 3, 4, 9, 10-A, 19-A, 23, and 
24 of the Constitution of the Islamic Republic of Pakistan, 1973, as well 
as section 24-A of the General Clauses Act, 1897, and are contrary to 
settled law laid down by the superior Courts. He further submitted that 
the amounts received by the petitioner company were lawful 
consideration for plots and not deposits under Companies (Invitation and 
Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 1987. Lastly, the learned counsel for the 
petitioner company submitted that no alternate, adequate, or effective

4 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
remedy is available, compelling recourse to this Court for redressal of 
grievances. 
7. 
Conversely, the learned counsel for the SECP contended that in 
March, 2021, the petitioner company was found, through social media, to 
be inviting money from the general public by using registration 
certificates for future housing and commercial projects and by offering 
financial benefits and a prize-based lucky draw; that such conduct is 
prohibited under section 84 of the Act 2017, which bars companies, other 
than authorized entities, from accepting deposits from the public. He also 
submitted that the petitioner company’s reliance on the Companies 
(Invitation and Acceptance of Deposits) Rules, 1987, is misconceived, as 
those rules were framed under the repealed Companies Ordinance, 1984 
and have no legal force under the Act 2017, even otherwise, those rules 
do not permit the petitioner company to collect deposits from the public. 
He further contended that the announcement of a lucky draw to attract 
funds amounts for an unlawful scheme under section 301 of the Act 
2017, as it involves the collection of money with the promise of future 
benefits, and that the petitioner company admitted the illegality of such 
scheme in its correspondence dated 12.04.2021, and allegedly misled the 
public by marketing its housing project and collecting funds without 
obtaining the required approvals from the GDA, which later declared the 
lucky draw illegal, cancelled the PP Permission, and sought regulatory 
action. He also submitted that these acts also violate the Punjab Housing 
Schemes and Land Sub-Divisions Rules, 2010, section 26 of the Act 
2017, and the petitioner company’s own MOA, as it was engaged in 
unauthorized and unlawful business activities beyond its permitted 
objects. He contended that the writ petitions are not maintainable 
because the impugned actions are merely statutory requirements, which 
are purely fact-finding and procedural in nature, and that during the 
pendency of these petitions, the investigation under the investigation 
order has already been concluded and the SECP acted strictly in 
accordance with the law.

5 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
8. 
I have heard the arguments of the learned counsel for the parties 
and perused the record.  
9. 
Perusal of the record reveals that the petitioner company is a duly 
registered company incorporated under the Act 2017, and holds a valid 
Certificate of Incorporation dated 19.10.2020, issued by the SECP. 
Clause-3 of MOA of the petitioner company shows that the principal 
objects of the petitioner company include the development of housing 
estates and all kinds of construction activities, as well as the 
management, maintenance, improvement, and construction of housing 
schemes, colonies, towns, apartments, plazas, hotels, restaurants, shops, 
hospitals, and multi-storey flats, along with other allied businesses. After 
its incorporation, the petitioner company approached the GDA seeking 
grant of PP Permission for a proposed project known as “La Villa De 
Paris Housing Scheme,” covering land measuring 18,817 Kanal and 05 
Marlas, situated at Mouza Adho Ray Qiyla, Nohad Singh, Chadiala 
Khurd And Chadiala Kalan, District Gujranwala. The record reflects that 
after due consideration, the GDA granted the petitioner company PP 
Permission through letter dated 25.08.2021, subject to certain terms and 
conditions, which are reproduced as under:- 
  “The subject permission shall be subject to the following 
conditions: 
a. 
… 
b. 
… 
c. 
It shall not be a permission to carry out any construction 
activities at the proposed site. 
d. It shall not permit marketing/ balloting /lucky draw/ sale-
purchase of plots or publicity of the scheme in any mode of 
communication. 
e. 
… 
f. 
You are directed to submit NOCs from Irrigation 
Department regarding construction of bridge on UCC 
and construction of road along UCC and Rajbah passing 
through the site and also Certificate from revenue 
department that the site proposed for the scheme is not 
notified by the Govt. for acquisition of any other public 
purpose before the approval of technical stage of subject

6 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
scheme. In case of failure, the conditional approval of 
Preliminary Planning Permission shall stand cancel.” 
10. 
The above referred conditions of PP Permission explicitly stated 
that no advertisement or public promotion of the proposed housing 
scheme project of the petitioner company is permitted in any medium 
unless and until the layout plan of the scheme is formally approved by 
the GDA. The purpose of this direction was to ensure that the public is 
not misled and that no publicity is made for the project that has not yet 
met the mandatory legal and regulatory requirements. The conditions 
also expressly stated that such approval must be supported by a valid No 
Objection Certificate (NOC) issued by the GDA. This restriction was 
imposed in the larger public interest, to maintain transparency, regulatory 
compliance, and to prevent unauthorized marketing of housing schemes 
before completion of the prescribed approval processes under the law. 
However, the petitioner company, through various modes of 
advertisements, invited general public to purchase certificates titled “Le 
Paris Registration Certificate,” to become entitled for investment in 
residential and commercial property schemes of the petitioner company 
in future, and participation in lucky draw for lucrative cash prizes. These 
promotional activities were not confined to a single forum but were 
widely circulated through print and electronic media, Facebook pages 
and groups, YouTube channels, and company’s Instagram handle. 
11. 
Resultantly, SECP took notice of the matter and collected relevant 
information 
and 
documentary 
material, 
including 
brochures, 
advertisements, and other related documents, to assess the legality and 
regulatory compliance of the petitioner company’s actions in light of the 
Act 2017, and observed that the petitioner company was issuing 
certificates having monetary value and offering a lucky draw to induce 
public investment. In view of the above circumstances and the material 
available on record, the SECP, while exercising its statutory powers 
under section 221 of the Act 2017, considered it necessary to inspect the

7 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
books of accounts of the petitioner company and other related 
documents. Accordingly, the SECP, based on material available, passed 
the impugned Inspection Order dated 24.03.2021 under section 221, 
directing the inspection of the books of accounts and other relevant 
record of the petitioner company to ascertain the true nature of its 
activities, and duly appointed Inspectors to carry out the inspection to 
collect all necessary documents and information for compliance of order 
and prepare the Inspection Report. 
12. 
The Inspectors in pursuance of the impugned Inspection Order 
dated 24.03.2021 proceeded with the matter, and issued letter dated 
25.03.2021 to the petitioner company requiring it to provide the books of 
accounts, record, and information, along with supporting documents, for 
inspection. On 26.03.2021, the inspection team visited registered office 
of the petitioner company in order to collect the record and had pre-
inspection meeting with the office bearer of the petitioner company. The 
petitioner company submitted reply dated 26.03.2021 to the letter dated 
25.03.2021 and sought three weeks to provide the relevant requisite 
information. On 29.03.2021, the Inspectors again sent a letter informing 
the petitioner company regarding their visit on 31.03.2021, and when the 
inspection team visited at the registered address of the petitioner 
company, its representative handed over a copy of a letter to the 
inspection team, wherein it was claimed that the impugned Inspection 
Order dated 24.03.2021 and letters issued by the inspection team are 
illegal, arbitrary and constitute abuse of power and they should be 
withdrawn in light of Articles 10 and 260 of the Constitution, and 
provided no record for inspection. On 07.04.2021, the inspection team 
again apprised the petitioner company demanding the requisite 
information. In response the petitioner company submitted letters along 
with partial record. Thereafter, the inspection team based on the 
available record and inspections conducted, recorded its findings vide 
impugned Inspection Report dated 06.05.2021, wherein it was recorded 
that the petitioner company solicited public funds through registration

8 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
certificates and announced monetary benefits, including lottery-based 
returns, in violation of the provisions of the Act 2017, and failed to 
produce complete books of accounts and mandatory records. The 
inspection team recommended that an unexplained sources of funds 
involving cash transactions of substantial magnitude, and breach of the 
MOA, require appropriate actions against the petitioner company under 
the relevant provisions of the Act 2017, including sections 84, 256 and 
500, and that the petitioner company be treated as a high-risk entity 
warranting further investigation.  
13. 
Based on the impugned Inspection Report dated 06.05.2021, the 
SECP issued the impugned Show-Cause Notice dated 21.05.2021 under 
section 256 of the Act 2017, forming a prima facie opinion that the 
petitioner company had solicited public participation through registration 
certificates carrying monetary benefits, including lottery-based returns, 
employed expressions 
attracting statutory prohibitions, effected 
substantial cash transactions, and claimed payments of nearly Rs. 1 
billion from unexplained sources despite negligible paid-up capital, and 
also failed to produce mandatory statutory and financial records. 
Considering the gravity of the alleged violations and the potential 
prejudice to shareholders and the general public, the SECP proposed to 
initiate investigation into the affairs of the petitioner company under 
section 256(1)(c) of the Act, after affording it an opportunity of being 
heard, and appointed inspectors for the purpose of investigation into 
affairs of the company. The SECP also initiated impugned proceedings 
under section 474 of the Act 2017 by issuing a notice to the petitioner 
company on the basis of non-compliance of the provisions of the Act 
2017, in violation of section 84 read with section 301 of the Act. Upon 
consideration of the material on record, including communications from 
the State Bank of Pakistan and the GDA, it was found that the petitioner 
company continued unlawful marketing and investment activities 
without requisite approvals, failed to refund amounts collected from the 
public, and persisted in promotional conduct expressly prohibited under

9 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
law. Consequently, the SECP directed the petitioner company and its 
directors to make good the defaults by refunding all amounts received 
from the public, to cease unlawful activities forthwith, to remove all 
promotional materials from every medium, and ensure full compliance of 
law, failing which, coercive action under the relevant provisions of the 
Act 2017 would be followed. It is pertinent to mention that the petitioner 
company filed review petition under section 32-B of SECP Act, 1997 
against the investigation order, which was dismissed vide impugned 
Order dated 12.01.2023. (W.P No.314/2023) 
14. 
During the pendency of these petitions, the SECP continued its 
statutory proceedings and, upon completion of a detailed investigation, 
prepared investigation report, which reveals that the petitioner company 
had raised substantial funds amounting to approximately Rs. 1.672 
billion through issuance of bearer registration certificates carrying 
guaranteed returns, a significant portion whereof remained outstanding 
and unpaid in clear disregard of the SECP’s directions issued under 
section 474 of the Act 2017. The certificates were structured and 
marketed as financial instruments promising the investors assured returns 
and lottery-based incentives, thereby constituting illegal deposit-taking 
in violation of section 84(1) of the Act. The investigation report further 
discloses serious accounting irregularities, including non-maintenance of 
proper books of accounts, misclassification of deposits as advances, non-
provision of material liabilities, cash transactions with directors in breach 
of section 211(4), disclaimer of audit opinion, and failure to lay audited 
financial statements before shareholders as required. It is also established 
that the petitioner company lacked requisite approvals and NOCs from 
the GDA and conducted its affairs on speculative assumptions without 
land ownership or lawful sanction, thereby endangering public interest. 
These cumulative findings led the investigation team to conclude that the 
petitioner company had been carrying on unlawful activities, failed to 
manage its business on sound commercial principles, and rendered itself 
liable to regulatory actions.

10 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
15. 
Furthermore, the entire record and the proceedings before the 
SECP, clearly demonstrate that the petitioner company was fully aware 
of and actively participated in all the proceedings initiated by the SECP. 
The record shows that the petitioner company duly responded and 
submitted its replies to the notices, which demonstrate that the petitioner 
was afforded ample opportunity to be heard and was not taken by 
surprise at any stage of the proceedings. Therefore, it cannot be said that 
the actions taken by the SECP were unilateral or that the petitioner 
company was denied presenting its case, as it remained engaged 
throughout the process and addressed all matters raised by the SECP and 
regarding the  procedures adopted by the regulatory body the SECP, this 
Court does not see any malice or ulterior motive on part of the SECP or 
violation of the principle of natural justice. 
16. 
For the reasons stated above, the issues raised in the present 
petitions are deeply intertwined with disputed questions of facts, which 
are already subject to adjudication before the competent regulatory 
authority. The proceedings initiated by the SECP against the petitioner 
company are sub judice before, where the factual controversy, 
evidentiary record, and statutory implications are yet to attain finality. To 
the extent of the impugned Inspection Order dated 24.03.2021, 
Inspection Report dated 06.05.2021, Show Cause Notice dated 
21.05.2021  issued under section 256 of the Act 2017, and proceedings 
initiated under section 474 of the Act, these petitions have become 
infructuous, as the final investigation has since been concluded and a 
comprehensive investigation report has already been submitted by the 
SECP before this Court. The petitioner company has an opportunity to 
raise objections to the investigation report under the Act 2017 read 
together with the SECP Act, 1997, which provide statutory remedies to 
any aggrieved party by any action taken by the SECP pursuant to 
investigation report.

11 
Writ Petitions No.3566/2021, 4598/2022 & 314/2023. 
 
 
17. 
In view of above discussion, all the afore-titled writ petitions bears 
no merits, therefore, the same stands dismissed. The parties may avail 
the remedies available to them under the Act 2017 and SECP Act, 1997 
before the relevant forum,if so, advised. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     (INAAM AMEEN MINHAS) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
           JUDGE 
 
 
Announced in open Court on 05.01.2026. 
 
 
 
                                                           (KHADIM HUSSAIN SOOMRO) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
          JUDGE 
 
 
R.Anjam.
